newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania ex-premier launches bid to unseat Iliescu.
newsitem.headline: Romania ex-premier launches bid to unseat Iliescu.

text.p: Romania's first post-communist premier, Petre Roman, began his presidential campaign on Friday with a colourful rally to showcase the left-of-centre programme he hopes will unseat President Ion Iliescu in November.
The charismatic Roman, 50, roused supporters packing the hall that housed late Stalinist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu's last Communist Party congress.
He issued a challenge to Iliescu, who sacked him after anti-reform riots by gangs of miners five years ago.
"I joined the race for the president's job because the incumbent president and the present government said nothing more can be done," he told Social Democratic Union (USD) party members.
Five year after his fall, Roman basked in the lights of the cameras and presented himself as an outward-looking dynamic reformer with a human touch.
Romania, the only former communist country where leftwingers retained power after 1989, holds its third presidential and parliamentary polls on November 3.

Opinion polls place Roman third in the presidential race, after Iliescu, his former ally during the revolution, and Emil Constantinescu, an academic who is running for the centrist opposition Democratic Convention bloc.

"The year 1996 is a turning point in the confrontation pitting conservative and anti-democratic forces against innovative forces," said Roman, who blames his dismissal five years ago on a putsch plotted by communists opposed to reforms.
Roman's bid for the presidency is expected to boost the performance of the USD, a union formed last year with a smaller Social Democratic party, which placed third in local elections in June.

Roman, who won Western sympathy for his ambitious reform drive when in power, was feted by cheerleaders with pom-poms and teenagers with bandanas reading "Roman for president" as he outlined his programme for Romania up to the year 2000.
"Our political programme is based on concrete solutions aimed at ending the crisis," he said.
Appealing to young voters, entrepreneurs and investors, he promised to create new jobs by boosting investment and to fight inflation through "rational fiscal and monetary policies."
"I pledge to mediate for the formation of a government capable of respecting the fundamental principles of a market economy," said Roman.

"By the year 2000 Romania has the chance to eradicate poverty and meet the conditions of integration into the European Union," said Roman, who is known as a staunch campaigner for Romania's NATO and EU membership bid.

Roman, a former hydraulics professor who speaks fluent English, French and Spanish, refrained from attacking Iliescu personally, despite a legacy of bitterness against the former communist functionary who won elections in 1990 and 1992.
"My only rival is poverty, the plight of the country and its people, not one of the presidential hopefuls," he said.
